scope: L01 actual implemented English counterpart and all shared Python source files. Chinese/traditional code parity is checked separately. This is not a review of all 39 chapters or empirical teaching efficacy.

reader.experience: Experienced enterprise frontend engineer; independently builds frontend applications; comfortable with JS, Promise and async/await; basic TypeScript. No Python, backend implementation, database or operations practice.
reader.goal: Eventually independently build, deploy and maintain a real backend. No fixed learning schedule. Wants careful incremental explanation, not API lists or unexplained copying.

state.completed_L00: Learner can save and run a .py script; understands literals versus names, basic assignment and print calls, sequential execution, error-line diagnosis for NameError and SyntaxError. Can use the exact uv --no-project Python 3.13 command. No functions, imports, loops, containers, exception handling, project files, testing frameworks or web server knowledge is assumed.

current_lesson.content:
--- title: "Names, Values, and Basic Operations" description: "Move beyond your first script by understanding Python name binding, basic values, arithmetic, None, strings, and explicit conversion. Practice prediction, diagnosis, and an independent calculation script without premature project setup." --- import { getScalarExample } from '@/lib/js2py-examples' ## 1. From running a script to explaining a calculation In L00, you saved and ran a `.py` file, distinguished a quoted string from an unquoted name, and located a problem using an error message. Now we will process a little data: turn a task title and an estimated number of minutes into a readable time estimate. Even this small requirement exposes differences that cannot simply be borrowed from JS. Can `"95"` participate in addition directly? Does dividing integers produce an integer? Does assigning one name to another establish a reactive relationship? What should represent an unassigned task owner? This chapter answers these questions one at a time rather than substituting a syntax table for explanation. You do not have to finish in one sitting. Each checkpoint leaves you with a small, understood, runnable result. ### Chapter contract | Item | Agreement | | --- | --- | | Prerequisite | Complete L00: save and run a script; explain names, literals, assignment, `print`, and sequential execution | | New capabilities | Trace name bindings; distinguish basic values; calculate, compare, convert, and format; diagnose two input-related errors | | Independent exit task | Predict before running; explain why reassignment does not change past output; write a reading-time script without the answer and verify changed inputs | | Not required here | Containers, loops, branches, function definitions, scope, annotations, exception handling, modules, environment configuration, test frameworks, or web services | **Calling a built-in function does not require learning to define functions yet. Observing an error does not require learning `try/except`.** We introduce only what the current problem needs. ### Files and execution Type the examples yourself, or download the [L01 examples and separate answers](/learning-assets/js2py/u01-scalars.zip). Extract the archive, open the `u01-scalars` folder in your editor, and place your terminal in that folder. Each named `.py` file is an independent script; it does not require a previous file to have run. Reuse the command already verified in L00. For the first file: ```bash uv run --no-project --python 3.13 python bindings.py ``` Replace only the final filename as you reach other examples, such as `numbers.py`. This chapter uses CPython 3.13 without third-party Python packages. You do not create a project or install test tools. If `uv` is not available, return to the [L00 local execution steps](/en/docs/js2py/module-00-python-introduction) rather than starting a second installation approach. Files under `errors` **fail intentionally**; `solutions` contains answers to open after your own attempt. These files are not a service that must be started together. ## 2. Name binding is not a fixed-type storage box ### 2.1 Predict the three lines first File: `bindings.py`. {getScalarExample('bindings.py')} Expected: ```text 30 45 30 ``` Read assignment in two steps: evaluate the right-hand side, then bind the name on the left to the resulting object. Here, “object” means a runtime value with its own type and behavior; it does not assume you can write a class. | Statement executed | Current binding of `minutes` | Current binding of `saved_minutes` | New output | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `minutes = 30` | Integer `30` | Not yet bound | None | | `saved_minutes = minutes` | Integer `30` | The same integer object | None | | `print(minutes)` | Integer `30` | Integer `30` | `30` | | `minutes = 45` | Integer `45` | Still integer `30` | None | | The last two prints | Integer `45` | Integer `30` | `45`, then `30` | `minutes = 45` changes the name's binding. It does not mutate the original integer `30` into `45`. Nor is `saved_minutes` a formula that keeps reading `minutes`. It reads the right-hand side once when that assignment executes. Do **not** infer that “Python assignment automatically copies data.” Two names can refer to the same object. This example has no change propagating to the other name because we rebind a name, and integers themselves are immutable. L02 will explore shared references and container mutation separately. You do not need memory addresses, `id()`, or caching rules to explain this program. The first line already printed in the terminal will not become `45` either. `print` performs an output action at that moment; it is not a UI subscription to a changing name. ### 2.2 Use your frontend experience without overextending the analogy Reassignment here can be compared with JS `let`. However, ordinary Python assignment has no `let`/`const` declaration keyword, and it does not acquire JS `const` binding restrictions. This is a naming convention, not syntax enforcement: ```python case=constant_convention MINUTES_PER_SESSION = 25 MINUTES_PER_SESSION = 30 print(MINUTES_PER_SESSION) ``` Output: ```text 30 ``` Uppercase communicates that the author intends a constant. The interpreter does not prevent the reassignment above. Team conventions are not runtime guarantees. This course uses `snake_case` for ordinary names, such as `saved_minutes`. Names are case-sensitive: `minutes` and `Minutes` differ. They cannot begin with a digit or use a reserved keyword such as `class`. Avoid using `print`, `str`, or `int` for your own variables, because that shadows the built-in functionality you will call later. Local scope belongs in the functions chapter. **Checkpoint A:** Without running, explain which outputs change if the first `30` becomes `20`. If you still expect `saved_minutes` to become `45` automatically, reconstruct the binding table before moving on to operators. ## 3. Values have types; names can be rebound ### 3.1 Similar appearance, different values | Expression | Type name | Meaning here | | --- | --- | --- | | `30` | `int` | An integer used in integer calculations | | `30.0` | `float` | A floating-point number with finite precision | | `"30"` | `str` | Two characters of text; looking numeric does not make it an integer | | `True`, `False` | `bool` | Boolean values, with capitalized first letters | | `None` | `NoneType` | The dedicated object used for absence, with meaning assigned by your application | Calling these “basic single values” distinguishes this chapter from the next chapter's containers; it is not new Python declaration syntax. Strings also have sequence behavior, which we will study later. `type(value)` lets you inspect the current value's type. Learn to call it here; metaclasses are not a prerequisite. File: `scalar_types.py`. {getScalarExample('scalar_types.py')} Expected: ```text ``` `print(type(30))` calls the inner `type` first, then passes its result to the outer `print`. The word `class` in the output is how the type is displayed, not an instruction to define a class first. At the end, `minutes` first refers to an integer and then to a string. The language permits this. But permission to rebind a name to another type does not make all mixed-type operations valid. As a program grows, one name carrying conflicting meanings becomes harder to understand. Real code often uses `raw_minutes` for the original text and `minutes` for the converted integer. ### 3.2 An expression, its result, and output are different things `30 + 15` is an expression that evaluates to a value. `total = 30 + 15` keeps its result; `print(total)` writes the result to the terminal. Writing `30 + 15` on a script line does not automatically echo it as some interactive consoles would. The examples retain `print` so you can observe results, not because calculations need it to work. ## 4. Arithmetic: learn the result rules, not just the symbols ### 4.1 Start with positive numbers, then inspect the type File: `numbers.py`. Predict the first seven lines before considering the final three edge cases. {getScalarExample('numbers.py')} Complete output: ```text 9 5 14 3.5 3 1 49 3.0 -4 1 ``` | Expression | Result | Explanation | | --- | --- | --- | | `7 + 2`, `7 - 2`, `7 * 2` | `9`, `5`, `14` | Addition, subtraction, multiplication | | `7 / 2` | `3.5` | True division; `/` returns a floating-point result even with two integers | | `7 // 2` | `3` | Floor division, not retaining the fractional part | | `7 % 2` | `1` | The remainder paired with floor division | | `7 ** 2` | `49` | Exponentiation; do not substitute `^` | | `7.0 // 2` | `3.0` | A floored result, but a floating-point operand keeps the result a `float` | Similarly, `8 / 2` is `4.0`, not `4`. The important part of `//` is the floor rule; do not memorize it as “division that returns an int.” These rules are documented in Python's [numeric types](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/stdtypes.html#numeric-types-int-float-complex). Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition and subtraction. Use parentheses when intent could be unclear: ```python case=precedence print(2 + 3 * 4) print((2 + 3) * 4) print(-(3 ** 2)) print((-3) ** 2) ``` Output: ```text 14 20 -9 9 ``` The final two lines mean “square, then negate” and “square the whole negative number.” Express your intent with parentheses rather than memorizing the full precedence table now. Division by zero raises `ZeroDivisionError` instead of producing JavaScript Number's `Infinity`. Do not use zero as the divisor in our time conversion. ### 4.2 Negative numbers expose the “remove the decimal part” misconception `-7 / 2` is `-3.5`. Flooring moves toward the smaller integer, so `-7 // 2` is `-4`, not `-3`. Its paired remainder is `1`, because: ```text -7 = (-4) * 2 + 1 ``` For integers with a nonzero divisor, quotient and remainder satisfy `a == (a // b) * b + a % b`. A nonzero Python integer remainder has the divisor's sign. JS `%` uses a different negative-number remainder rule: JS `-7 % 2` is `-1`. Check the [Python expression reference](https://docs.python.org/3.13/reference/expressions.html#binary-arithmetic-operations) and [JS remainder documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Remainder) when you need to distinguish them. Our deliverable uses positive minutes. You do not need negative modulo to implement the task; the experiment prevents the incorrect rule that `//` merely cuts off fractional digits. ### 4.3 Large integers and fractions: different precision issues This static comparison illustrates the language boundary. This chapter's acceptance uses local CPython rather than the webpage runner. ```javascript case=integer_precision console.log(2 ** 53); console.log(2 ** 53 + 1); ``` ```python case=integer_precision print(2 ** 53) print(2 ** 53 + 1) ``` Python output: ```text 9007199254740992 9007199254740993 ``` JS Number prints `9007199254740992` twice. Python `int` is not constrained by JS Number's safe-integer range; it preserves integer precision within available resources. This does not imply unlimited computation or memory. JS also has a separate `BigInt` type, so this comparison does not mean JS cannot handle large integers. See [Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number/MAX_SAFE_INTEGER). A `float` cannot represent every decimal fraction exactly: ```python case=float_precision print(0.1 + 0.2) print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) ``` Output: ```text 0.30000000000000004 False ``` `==` compares values for equality; the next section introduces it more fully. This is not a random calculation failure: binary floating-point approximations produce an observable difference. Displaying two decimal places does not make the arithmetic exact. We use time estimates rather than financial settlement for practice; exact-decimal approaches come after their prerequisites. The official [floating-point tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3.13/tutorial/floatingpoint.html) explains the limitation. **Checkpoint B:** Explain what `95 // 60` and `95 % 60` represent and why `7.0 // 2` includes `.0`. If you remember only the outputs rather than the rules, try another pair of numbers on paper. ## 5. Comparisons, Boolean values, and absence ### 5.1 `=` binds; `==` compares values `minutes = 30` is assignment. `minutes == 30` produces a Boolean without changing the name. Python has no `===`. However, Python `==` is not simply JS loose equality or JS strict equality: it does not turn `"30"` into an integer here, yet different numeric types can compare equal. This independent script combines comparisons and absence checks. File: `boolean_none.py`. {getScalarExample('boolean_none.py')} Expected: ```text True False True True True False None True False ``` Read the results individually: - `30 == 30.0` is `True`: different types, equal numeric values. - `"30" == 30` is `False`: numeric-looking text is not automatically converted for this comparison. - `True == 1` is `True`: `bool` is a subtype of `int`, so Boolean values are related to `1` and `0` in numeric comparisons. Know the boundary, but keep concepts such as “completed” and “quantity” distinct in application code. Do not use this relationship as an excuse to skip data checks. - `!=` means not equal; `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=` mean less than, less than or equal, greater than, and greater than or equal. These produce Boolean results. They do not automatically print a conclusion or redirect execution. For now, observe Boolean values. `if`, `and`, `or`, and general truthiness are not yet taught. You do not need conditional statements to handle these results, and should not assume that `bool("False")` parses Boolean text. ### 5.2 `None` is different from a name that does not exist Here we agree that `assignee = None` means “no assignee yet.” The assignment has bound the name; reading `assignee` is valid and returns `None`. Keep these states separate: | State | Interpretation in this example | | --- | --- | | `assignee = None` | The name exists; our convention says there is no assignee yet | | `assignee = ""` | The name exists and holds an empty string; whether an empty name is allowed needs another rule | | `assignee = "None"` | Four letters of ordinary text, not the absence object | | Reading `assignee` without ever binding it | An unbound name, producing the `NameError` explored in L00 | `0` and `False` have their own meanings too; they are not alternative spellings of `None`. Treat `value is None` here as a narrowly defined check: is this value the dedicated `None` object? It is not string matching, and it does not treat an empty string as `None`. More generally, `is` concerns object identity, not another strict-equality operator. **Do not use `is` to compare numeric or string contents.** Further identity questions belong with containers and references. See the [None constant](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/constants.html#None) and [PEP 8's comparison recommendation](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#programming-recommendations). ## 6. Strings: cleaning text does not mutate the original A task title may contain leading and trailing spaces. We want a cleaned title for display while retaining the original for comparison. Single and double quotes both delimit ordinary Python strings; these delimiter characters are not automatically included in the output. JS backtick templates cannot be copied unchanged. The f-string introduced later is our interpolation tool here. First understand `raw_title.strip()`: the name after the dot is a string method, and the parentheses call it now. With no arguments here, it returns a string without leading and trailing whitespace. It does not delete internal spaces or mutate `raw_title`. Calling an existing method does not require defining classes or methods first. File: `strings.py`. {getScalarExample('strings.py')} Expected: ```text [ Read Python basics ] [Read Python basics] 18 Python basics It is "Python". first second ``` The first two lines concatenate square brackets around the text to make spaces visible. Those brackets are ordinary characters inside quotes, **not list syntax**. `title` receives the cleaned result; `raw_title` still retains spaces on both sides. Strings are immutable. A method can return processed text, and you must use or keep that result. Writing only `raw_title.strip()` and then printing `raw_title` does not change what the name subsequently refers to. `+` joins text when both operands are strings; it does not add a separating space for you. `len(title)` returns the length. All characters in this example are ASCII, and `Read Python basics` has 18, including spaces. Python `str` length counts Unicode code points, not necessarily visible characters; JS `String.length` counts UTF-16 code units. Unicode character counting is not an exit requirement here, but this simple example must not be generalized to all emoji or display widths. `'It is "Python".'` uses outer single quotes around text containing double quotes. Inside a double-quoted string, `\"` is another way to include a double quote. `\n` represents a newline, so the final `print` produces two lines of text. To include a literal backslash, write `\\`. See the [text introduction](https://docs.python.org/3.13/tutorial/introduction.html#text) and [string methods](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/stdtypes.html#string-methods). Learn boundary cleanup, concatenation, and length here. A catalogue of dozens of methods, indexing, and slicing can wait. ## 7. Explicit conversion: looking numeric is not being numeric ### 7.1 Decide whether you want arithmetic or concatenation `"30" + "15"` is `"3015"`; `30 + 15` is `45`. Both are valid, but solve different problems. `"30" + 15` does not work directly: Python will not choose which side to convert for you. In this chapter, the built-ins `int`, `float`, and `str` obtain an integer, a floating-point number, and a text representation respectively. File: `conversions.py`. {getScalarExample('conversions.py')} Expected: ```text 45 3.5 3 -3 Minutes: 30 ``` `int(raw_minutes)` reads `"30"` and returns integer `30`. It does not transform the original string in place; `minutes` binds to the conversion result. The following addition therefore performs arithmetic. The final line converts the integer to text before concatenating text. `int(3.9)` and `int(-3.9)` discard the fractional part, truncating toward zero. This is neither rounding to the nearest integer nor the floor rule used by `//`. Negative numbers distinguish them: `int(-3.9)` is `-3`, whereas `-7 // 2` is `-4`. ### 7.2 Diagnose two failures instead of hiding them First experiment: `errors/text_plus_number.py`. {getScalarExample('errors/text_plus_number.py')} There is no normal output. The final error line resembles: ```text TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str ``` Inspect line 2. The argument expression must be evaluated before `print` receives it. Addition fails first, so `print` never receives a result. The later `finished` line does not appear either. The error is an unsupported combination of types for this operation, not an inability of `print` to display numbers. Before fixing it, ask what is required: 45 minutes or the text `3015`? Here we need arithmetic, so convert the original text to an integer rather than converting `15` to text just to suppress an error. Section 10 makes this repair an exercise. Second experiment: `errors/invalid_integer.py`. {getScalarExample('errors/invalid_integer.py')} Again, there is no normal output. The final line resembles: ```text ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5' ``` `int` can process a string representing an integer, but `"3.5"` is not such a string. This differs from `int(3.5)`, which already receives a floating-point number and can truncate it using the rule above. Do not silently replace this with `int(float(raw_sessions))` just to make the error disappear. If the value represents study sessions, whether 3.5 sessions is meaningful is a requirements question. Converting to float and truncating can discard the user's intent. You might require another integer input or explicitly support fractions; complete validation and error responses belong after branches, exceptions, and server fundamentals. Your task now is to record the error type, source line, actual value type, and intended result. We deliberately do not wrap the code in `try/except`. See the [built-ins including `int` and `float`](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/functions.html#int) and [TypeError / ValueError](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/exceptions.html#ValueError). **Successful conversion is not complete business validation.** `int("-5")` produces integer `-5`, but whether an estimated duration may be negative is a separate rule. The following script handles trusted values we write into its source. It is not a backend ready for arbitrary public requests. **Checkpoint C:** Without running, distinguish `int("3.5")`, `int(3.5)`, and `"3" + "5"`. For a failure, explain which step fails instead of merely copying the last error line. ## 8. f-strings produce text, not reactive views `"Minutes: " + str(minutes)` works, but repeated manual concatenation makes it easy to omit a space or conversion. An f-string prefixes the quoted string with `f` and embeds expressions inside braces. Python evaluates them when that line executes and places their formatted results into a new string. File: `formatting.py`. {getScalarExample('formatting.py')} Expected: ```text Estimate: 95 minutes Estimate: 95 minutes Estimate: 120 minutes Decimal hours: 1.58 1.5833333333333333 ``` `report` was constructed when `minutes` was `95`. Rebinding `minutes` to `120` does not rewrite an existing string. Constructing a new f-string in a later print reads the new value. This resembles an ordinary string already produced by a JS template literal, not a Vue computed property or a subsequent React render. In `{hours:.2f}`, `hours` before the colon is the value; `.2f` requests fixed-point formatting with two decimal places. It changes the generated text, not `hours`. The final line still displays the original floating-point result. Formatting is not exact financial arithmetic or a business rounding policy. If you omit the opening `f`, braces remain literal text instead of interpolating a name. See the [output tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3.13/tutorial/inputoutput.html#formatted-string-literals) and [format specification](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/string.html#format-specification-mini-language). Mastering the entire formatting language is not required here. ## 9. Connect the pieces: a task estimate script Only now do we combine several operations in a complete file. Inputs are written directly in the source: no form, HTTP request, file reading, or database. File: `task_estimate.py`. {getScalarExample('task_estimate.py')} Run in the directory containing that file: ```bash uv run --no-project --python 3.13 python task_estimate.py ``` Expected: ```text Task: Read Python basics Estimate: 1h 35m Decimal hours: 1.58 ``` ### Follow the data | Step | Input | Result | Responsibility | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Read source constants | Padded title and `"95"` | Two strings | Preserve the original representation | | Clean | `raw_title` | `"Read Python basics"` | Remove surrounding whitespace, not internal spaces | | Convert | `raw_minutes` | Integer `95` | Enable numeric operations | | Decompose | `95` and `60` | Hours `1`, remaining minutes `35` | Express time using quotient and remainder | | Display | Title, hours, minutes, and division result | Three text lines | Format without changing calculated values | `hours` is the whole-hour portion; `minutes` is what remains, not the original input reused as a remainder. Decimal hours `1.58` is an approximation, not “1 hour and 58 minutes.” This is why you must explain units rather than accept anything that looks numeric. ### Make two changes yourself 1. Change `raw_minutes` to `"125"`. Predict first, then confirm `2h 5m` and `2.08` decimal hours. 2. Change it to `"60"`. Expect `1h 0m` and `1.00`. A zero remainder is not a reason to hard-code the entire output line. Restore `"95"` afterward. This script does not check empty titles, negative durations, or enormous numbers, and it receives no network data. It is an explained language exercise, not a product with completed server-side input validation. **Checkpoint D:** Close the lesson and describe “original text → converted values → calculation → display.” Return to the relevant section for any line you cannot explain instead of memorizing the whole program at once. ## 10. Graduated practice: predict, repair, then build independently Answers start collapsed. Understanding an answer is not a substitute for doing the work. In particular, printing the expected output as a hard-coded string does not satisfy a calculation task. ### Exercise A: predict bindings and a string snapshot ```python case=exercise_snapshot minutes = 30 saved_minutes = minutes label = f"Plan: {minutes}" minutes = minutes + 15 print(saved_minutes) print(minutes) print(label) ``` Write the three expected lines on paper. Explain why `minutes = minutes + 15` is not a mathematical equation. Then save it as `prediction.py` and verify using the same execution command.
After predicting, reveal the explanation ```text 30 45 Plan: 30 ``` The right-hand side reads the old value `30`, computes `45`, and then rebinds the name on the left. It does not require old and new values to be equal simultaneously. `saved_minutes` still refers to the old integer; `label` is the already constructed string. These names are not an automatically synchronized state-management system.
### Exercise B: repair the requirement, not just the exception Reopen `errors/text_plus_number.py`. It must print integer `45`, followed by `finished`. Keep the original `raw_minutes = "30"` and add a name for the converted value. Do not hard-code `45` or convert `15` into a string. After fixing it, change the input to `"50"`. Expect `65`, not `5015` or the original `45`.
After your repair and variation, reveal the reference File: `solutions/fix_minutes.py`. {getScalarExample('solutions/fix_minutes.py')} Expected output for the original input: ```text 45 finished ``` Conversion occurs before addition, repairing the type combination while satisfying the goal of calculating minutes. If the input becomes `"later"`, conversion still fails. This exercise does not require premature exception recovery logic.
### Exercise C: build a reading plan from an empty file Create `reading_plan.py` yourself and start with just these known values: ```python case=exercise_inputs raw_topic = " Python names " raw_sessions = "4" minutes_per_session = 25 ``` Meet these requirements: 1. Keep the original inputs, remove surrounding whitespace from the topic, and convert the session count. 2. Compute total duration from the count and minutes per session rather than writing the answer directly. 3. Decompose the total into hours and remaining minutes. 4. Produce the following three lines using only L00 and this chapter. ```text Topic: Python names Sessions: 4 Total: 100 minutes (1h 40m) ``` Run your own file, not the provided solution as a substitute for acceptance: ```bash uv run --no-project --python 3.13 python reading_plan.py ``` Now vary the inputs. With `"5"` sessions, expect `125 minutes (2h 5m)`. With topic `" Read slowly "`, expect `Read slowly`. No calculation code should need to change. Finally introduce a failure: set the count to `"many"`, predict the error type, and locate the conversion line. Explain why conversion is impossible; you do not need to catch the exception. Restore valid input after diagnosis.
After independent completion and variations, reveal the solution File: `solutions/reading_plan.py`. {getScalarExample('solutions/reading_plan.py')} The blank lines separate input, processing, and output for readability; they introduce no execution mechanism. `sessions` keeps the integer, multiplication produces `total_minutes`, and hours and remainder are calculated from it. A changed input therefore flows through the next execution. Different names are fine if the requirements are met. Compare your reasoning with the answer rather than demanding identical spelling.
## 11. Evidence for moving on, not a completion checkbox You are ready for the next chapter when you can independently: - Predict reassignment effects on the current name, another previously bound name, and an already generated string. - Explain `30`, `30.0`, `"30"`, `False`, and `None`, without confusing an unbound name with `None`. - Distinguish `/`, `//`, and `%`; explain negative flooring and floating-point approximation without treating two-decimal display as exact arithmetic. - Choose concatenation or arithmetic based on the requirement and explain the difference between the TypeError and ValueError experiments. - Write the reading plan from an empty file, pass input variations, and identify the lack of public-input validation. For anything that still requires the answer, return to the corresponding experiment. You do not need to memorize every exception, string method, or precedence rule. ### Returning after a break Before leaving, record the last successful file and output, one line you cannot yet explain, and one input to change next time. On returning, predict that change and run it. You do not need to reinstall the environment or reread the entire chapter. Next, **L02: Containers, References, and Mutation** will assemble single values into task data and examine shared references carefully. The website preserves historical URLs. Modules 00 and 01 now follow the new contracts; later pages are still being migrated. The old module 02 on modules is not the new L02, so do not mistake old website numbering for an already implemented prerequisite sequence. ## 12. Official references for further checks Use documentation to answer a specific question, not as a replacement for the lesson. The relevant sections already link numeric, string, exception, and formatting references. Also keep these available: - [Python assignment statements](https://docs.python.org/3.13/reference/simple_stmts.html#assignment-statements): right-hand evaluation, binding, and the distinction from mutation. - [Python data model](https://docs.python.org/3.13/reference/datamodel.html#objects-values-and-types): objects, types, values, and immutability; reading the whole reference is not required now. - [Python comparisons](https://docs.python.org/3.13/reference/expressions.html#comparisons): why numeric equality and object identity answer different questions.
